title: DATE: build a date from parts

screens.prompt: Column E wants the raised date as a real date number built from the year, month and day in B2:D2, so start with INV-2001 in E2.

hints.syntax: DATE takes year, month, day in that order: =DATE(B2,C2,D2).
hints.func-date: All three parts belong in one call; splitting them across two DATE calls adds two serials together.
hints.require-ref: Read the year, month and day from row 2, so the formula fills down to the other invoices.
hints.value: 2024, 3 and 1 build 45352, which is 1 March 2024. A nearby serial means a part came from the wrong column.
hints.error: A part stored as text returns #VALUE!, because DATE cannot build a serial from a label.

reject.why: the serial typed in by hand, which is the number DATE exists to save you from knowing
two parts are not a date — DATE needs the year, the month and the day
the parts typed in, so a corrected month in column C never reaches the date
the row below, so the formula no longer reads the year cell it is meant to build from
March's year and month with April's day, which lands on 15 March instead of 1 March
dividing the date away leaves #DIV/0! in the cell
the closing bracket is missing, so nothing runs

screens.prompt: In B3, build the first day of the month after the statement month in B2: March means April.

hints.syntax: The month can be an expression: =DATE(2024,B2+1,1) asks for April when B2 holds 3.
hints.func-date: Keep the +1 inside the call, where the year and the roll-over stay Excel's job.
hints.require-ref: Pass B2 rather than a typed 3, then add the one inside the brackets.
hints.value: March is 45352 and April has 31 days, so 1 April 2024 is 45383. A result of 45352 means the month never moved.
hints.error: A month of 13 rolls into the next year instead of failing, so an answer a year out points at the year argument.

reject.why: the first of the statement month, 45352, rather than the month after it
day zero is the day before the first, so this is the last day of March, 45382
the right answer with the month typed in, so a February statement still reports April
the serial typed in rather than built, so nothing rolls over when the month changes
no day argument, so DATE has nothing to build the first of the month from
dividing the date away leaves #DIV/0! in the cell
the closing bracket is missing, so nothing runs

docs.explain:
A date in Excel is a serial number: the count of days since the end of 1899, with 1 January 1900 as day 1. The grid stores that serial, and a formatted date is only what the cell draws. DATE builds the serial from three ordinary numbers, a year, a month and a day, and hands back a real date that sorts and subtracts.

The first screen wants 1 March 2024 in E2, which is serial 45352 built from 2024, 3 and 1. The second asks for the first day of April, so the month argument holds B2+1. DATE rolls the parts over instead of returning an error: month 13 is January of the next year, and day 0 is the day before the first.

That behaviour saves a table of month lengths. The first of next month is the current month plus one, and the last day of this month is day zero of the next. Expressions work in any part, which is how B2+1 becomes April.

errors.text: A part is text that does not read as a number, so DATE has nothing to build the serial from.
A negative year, or parts that push the result past 31 December 9999, fall outside the serials Excel holds.
A month built as B2+2 rolls into the following month without an error, so 1 May appears where 1 April was asked for.

docs.atWork: A finance export with the year, month and day in three columns, turned into one date column the ledger can sort and age.
docs.outcome: Build a real date from three numbers and let DATE roll the overflow.
docs.teaches: DATE, and how a date is stored as a number

seo.title: DATE in Excel: build a date from parts
seo.description: A date is a serial number counting days since 1899. DATE turns a year, a month and a day into one, and rolls month 13 over to January of the next year.
